whatTheyArgued: What the snip says is Hermann Jacobi's account (SBE 45, 1895 introduction), not Mahavira's words. Jacobi conjectures that Mahavira set up the Syadvada in opposition to the agnostic Sanjaya: one may affirm a thing's existence from one point of view (syat asti), deny it from another (syat nasti), and affirm both at different times; to affirm both from the same viewpoint at once, the thing is unspeakable (avaktavya). Jacobi presents this as the 'Saptabhanginaya' and speculates it silenced rivals. I read the passage and window; I did not read any Jaina sutra text of Mahavira's.

scholarship.ref: Wikipedia 'Anekantavada' (fetched; weak source, used only for the standard historiography, not as scholarship)
scholarship.supports: anekantavada traced to Mahavira's teaching but the term coined by Siddhasena Divakara; syadvada and nayavada (partial viewpoints) developed later in the first millennium CE (Umasvati, Samantabhadra, Kundakunda); it cites Matilal and Dundas
scholarship.disputes: Implies that the saptabhangi formalization post-dates Mahavira, against Jacobi's attribution of it to him. No IEP/SEP page could be fetched, so no credible peer-reviewed source was read; Matilal and Dundas are named but unread.

ourUse: perspective.js: projects 'who holds what' from the log. Beliefs are indexed by HOLDER (Walton, Victor, the creature, the reader), kept apart rather than merged, with a 'via' chain for nested reports and replay at any cursor. Handle: 'a claim is true from a standpoint, standpoints kept apart rather than merged into one voice'.

bends.ours: Header 'Mahavira speaks' and manifest giver 'Mahavira' over a sentence from Jacobi's 1895 introduction.
bends.theirs: The words are Jacobi's interpretive summary and his hypothesis about Mahavira's motives; the saptabhangi attribution to Mahavira himself is disputed in the later literature.

bends.ours: A standpoint = a holder (person or narrator) who believes a claim; the log keeps each holder's belief.
bends.theirs: In syadvada the viewpoint is an aspect from which one thing is truly described (substance, place, time, mode: 'at different times' in the snip). Several viewpoints are each partly true of the same thing. A holder's say-so is a different matter (belief report, closer to what experiencer.js tracks).

bends.ours: Beliefs are held, not asserted by the reader unless witnessed; no sevenfold predication, no avaktavya (unspeakable) outcome.
bends.theirs: The snip's core: each statement carries a qualifier (syat), existence and non-existence both affirmable at different viewpoints, and a same-time conflict yields 'cannot be spoken'. perspective.js has no such qualified predication.

bends.ours: organ header comment opens with a first-person 'speaks' block and commentary in the archon's voice ('My teaching prioritizes...', 'I believe...'), generated text presented as the author's own words (perspective.js: 'I believe it could further explore the nuances of how these perspectives are... inter-related').

fix: compendium work: 'Jain teacher, to whom tradition ascribes anekantavada: reality has many aspects and a statement is true from a stated viewpoint. In Jacobi's 1895 account the syadvada qualifies each assertion (syat asti, syat nasti) by viewpoint. perspective.js borrows only the habit of not merging viewpoints; it indexes beliefs by who holds them, which is not what the naya doctrine indexes.'
